title: Pricing by hours per project for Dog walking
audience: Dog walkers who write quotes for walks, multi-dog rounds and recurring routes, and need a price that covers cost and earns a margin.
learningOutcomes: Calculate a cost per productive hour from the owner's own figures
Estimate project hours, including set-up, travel and checking time
Build a quote from hours, a rate and a margin, and state its basis and exclusions

instruction.heading: Why hours are the starting unit
instruction.body: A 30-minute walk takes longer than 30 minutes of working time. Travel between homes, pick-up and drop-off, toileting, fresh water, the drop-off message and the note after the walk all take time. Start from hours so that every walk shows its cost. A flat per-walk price with no hours behind it hides travel and waste, and it cannot be defended when an owner asks why a walk costs what it does. Vendor price guides show wide ranges by walk length (Airtasker, updated 19 May 2026), but a range does not tell you your own cost.

instruction.heading: Build the cost per productive hour
instruction.body: Add the year's total running costs: vehicle running costs, insurance, phone and app fees, consumables such as bags and treats, any council permit fee, administration and equipment. If you employ walkers, add wages with on-costs such as leave and superannuation, and check which award or enterprise agreement applies to each worker. Divide by productive hours, meaning the hours you are walking dogs, not the hours you are on call. If a large share of your day goes on travel or admin, the cost per productive hour rises, and the price per walk has to rise with it. business.gov.au says on-costs belong in the hourly cost (1 October 2026).

instruction.heading: Estimate the hours
instruction.body: Break each booking into the walk, the travel to the next home, the pick-up and drop-off, and any admin. Add a named allowance for delays such as traffic, a dog that will not come back, or a late owner. Xero's small-business guide suggests 10 to 20 per cent for unexpected work (Xero Australia, 3 September 2026). That is a general figure, not a dog-walking figure, so size your own allowance from your records. After each walk, record the actual minutes and the reason for any difference. Carters Trade Leader, a New Zealand publisher, makes the same general point: use the gap between quoted and actual time to correct the next quote (1 October 2025).

instruction.heading: Turn hours into a price
instruction.body: Multiply the productive hours by the cost per productive hour, then add a margin for risk, such as a difficult dog, a long route or a tight window. Add the council permit cost as a named line once the fee is confirmed with the council. Apply your minimum charge. If an owner asks for a lower price, show which walk length, pick-up time or extra dog they are asking you to remove. That keeps the talk on the work rather than on the person.

instruction.heading: Keep the quote honest
instruction.body: A quote should state the walk length, the pick-up window, the number of dogs, the exclusions (for example, medication, grooming or a dog outside the agreed area), what the owner must provide, and how long the quote is valid. Do not show your internal cost per hour unless you choose to. Record every change to the route or the dog count, and re-quote when it changes. No Australian holiday or peak-season source was found, so do not set a surcharge figure from this lesson.

instruction.heading: Review your estimates
instruction.body: Compare estimated and actual minutes for at least the first ten walks of each type. If the gap is consistently above an agreed threshold, change the standard time, the margin or the scope rule. A pricing method is finished only when actual minutes match quoted minutes closely enough for the round to make money.

procedure: Gather the year's total running costs and the productive walking hours in the same period.
Divide total costs by productive hours to get the cost per productive hour.
Estimate each walk in minutes, including travel, pick-up, drop-off and admin, as a range.
Add a named allowance for delays and size it from your own records.
Multiply the hours by the cost per productive hour, then add the margin and any council permit cost.
Write the quote with walk length, dog count, exclusions and validity, and record actual minutes after each walk.

workedExamples.situation: Illustrative figures only, not market rates. A walker books four 30-minute walks in one Melbourne suburb in a single morning. Each walk is followed by 10 minutes of travel to the next home (three legs), and each home takes 5 minutes for pick-up and drop-off. Her cost per productive hour is $30 (illustrative), and her target margin on price is 25 per cent (illustrative).
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What are the working hours, the cost and the price for the round? What changes if one owner adds a 15-minute walk?
workedExamples.reasoning: The four walks take 120 minutes. The three travel legs take 30 minutes, and the four pick-ups and drop-offs take 20 minutes, so the round is 170 minutes, or 2.83 hours. The cost is 2.83 hours multiplied by $30, which is $85.00. A 25 per cent margin on price means the price is the cost divided by 0.75, which gives $113.33. If one owner adds a 15-minute walk, the round becomes 185 minutes, the cost becomes $92.50, and the price becomes $123.33, but only if the owner has agreed to the extra time and the quote's terms allow it. Nothing in this example is a sourced price.

equipmentAndPpe: Quote worksheet or spreadsheet with the cost per productive hour
Walk log for each booking, with estimated and actual minutes
Council permit fee schedule for each council you walk in
Standard walking kit as listed on your own safety checklist

commonErrors.error: Pricing from a per-walk listing price, or from the hourly wage alone
commonErrors.prevention: Include vehicle, insurance, phone, consumables, permit and admin in the cost per productive hour.

commonErrors.error: Counting booked hours as productive hours
commonErrors.prevention: Use the hours you spend walking dogs only.
Add travel as a named line on every round.

commonErrors.error: Quoting with no exclusions or pick-up window
commonErrors.prevention: State the exclusions, the window and the dog count on every quote.

commonErrors.error: Never comparing estimated and actual minutes
commonErrors.prevention: Record actual minutes after each walk and review the variance monthly.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Pricing guidance only. The Australian Consumer Law applies to pricing statements, and the ACCC says misleading price statements are prohibited (ACCC, 15 July 2026). State and territory fair-trading rules also apply and differ.

Pay rates, allowances and on-costs for employees may be set by an award or enterprise agreement. Check which one applies to each worker before using any wage figure. This lesson does not state those rates.

Council permit fees for commercial dog walking differ by council, and some are not settled. Yarra's fee is $153 on its council page and $155 on a government listing for 2025-26. Merri-bek lists $63.40 for 2026-27. Port Phillip's own page gives conflicting fee dates and no dollar amount. Confirm the current fee with each council before you add it to a quote.
No Australian source for holiday or peak-season pricing was found for dog walking. Do not add a surcharge figure from this lesson.

qualityStandard: Each quote shows walk length, pick-up window, dog count, exclusions, client inputs and validity.
The cost per productive hour is calculated from the walker's own records and dated.
Actual minutes are recorded for at least the first ten walks of each type and compared with the estimate.
No quote is issued without a margin decision and a council permit check where the number of dogs requires one.
documentationEvidence: Cost per productive hour worksheet, dated, with the source of each figure
Quote showing scope, hours basis, exclusions and validity
Walk log with estimated and actual minutes
Council permit check record for each council served, with the date checked
summary: Start every walk quote from minutes and travel, not from a listing price.
Cost per productive hour uses walking time, not the whole working day.
Name travel, pick-up and admin time on every quote.
Check council permits before you add dogs to a round.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which costs belong in the cost per productive hour for a dog walker?
options: The price the owner pays, plus the deposit and the late fee
The average walk price on a listing site in your suburb
Only the wage of the lowest-paid walker and no other cost
Vehicle, insurance, phone and app fees, consumables, permit and admin, divided by productive hours

knowledgeChecks.question: A walk is estimated at 30 minutes and takes 45. What is the right response?
options: Record the actual minutes, find the cause, and adjust the estimate and future quotes
Leave the estimate, since the owner has paid and the walk is finished
Reduce the walks for the next client and skip the water break
Raise the price for this owner only and no one else is charged more

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does a dog-walking quote need exclusions and a pick-up window?
options: To hide the margin from the owner and to keep the rates secret
To make the quote longer and fill up the page
To show what the price covers, so changes can be priced and disputes are reduced
To make the walk seem shorter than it is
